Title: Ignite 4 - Igniting Imagination
NewsSummary: "Ignite is an engaging, fast-paced platform for those seeking to present imaginative solutions to everyday problems," says Dr Asad Mian, paediatric emergentologist and CCIT organiser.
NewsContent:
"Imagination is more important than knowledge. Knowledge is limited. Imagination encircles the world."  - Albert Einstein

Acquiring a degree gives students a sense of completion - a belief that they now know enough to step out into the real world. However, as Einstein says, the usefulness of knowledge is subject to a constraint - a limitation that must be contested through the use of imagination and initiative.

If one remains bound by the restraints of the present and avoids asking the difficult questions such as: 'Why?', 'Why not?' and 'What if?'; one cannot begin to think about how to deal with everyday problems, let alone solve them.

The spirit of finding unconventional solutions and questioning conventional wisdom is what the Critical Creative Innovating Thinking (CCIT) forum's Ignite event is all about.

"Ignite is an engaging, fast-paced platform for those seeking to present imaginative solutions to everyday problems," says Dr Asad Mian, paediatric emergentologist and CCIT organiser. "Based at the Aga Khan University, the event gives each speaker just 5 minutes to address the audience and encourages people to find innovative answers to the world's problems."

Similar to its previous three editions, Ignite 4's speakers touched on a variety of topics within the broad categories of social wellbeing, biomedicine and healthcare on January 25, 2016. 

Entrepreneur Rumman Ahmed got the event off to a strong start with his exploration of what it takes to foster creativity. The talk was the perfect introduction to the evening as subsequent presentations demonstrated new approaches to tackling many other ever-present problems.

How do you inform young patients about their complicated illnesses? Lubaina Ehsan, a talented artist, who is currently a third year AKU medical student, has found a novel way - art. Her presentation showed how drawings could effectively create awareness about complicated illnesses and how well-designed pamphlets could enlighten young patients about various diseases. 

Dr Mirza Noor Ali, senior instructor at the Emergency Department, was more practical. In his fast-paced presentation he outlined why it's necessary for the public to be knowledgeable about first aid measures such as CPR or cardiopulmonary resuscitation. He reasoned that better knowledge about CPR would help increase the survival rate of a person with a suspected heart attack and decrease reliance on hospitals.

In the true spirit of sparking change, speakers weren't afraid to take on a topic as sensitive as sexual abuse, a taboo subject in conservative societies which means that it isn't discussed even though it has a very damaging impact on victims. Baila Shakaib, a fourth year medical student, took on the challenging topic and outlined how to help children recognise worrying behaviour and the steps they can take if they suffer abuse.

The audience next heard from Ali Allawala, CEO of the the Karachi Down Syndrome Program, a support network for the parents of children with Down syndrome. Mr Allawala shared his personal experiences of raising a child with Down's and highlighted how his daughter has an extra chromosome which gives her different abilities. His presentation challenged the prevailing stigma associated with the condition and urged people to change how they view disabilities.  

Other presenters at the session included Sarmad Soomar, a fourth year nursing student from AKU's School of Nursing and Midwifery, Hamza Iqbal, a final year student from the Lahore University of Management Sciences, Eve Ahmed, a journalist and writer from Oxford, United Kingdom, and Dr Qasim Raza, an AKU MBBS graduate currently working as a researcher at the Cleveland Clinic in the United States.

The interesting questions posed by the audience after every speech and the lively post-event discussion were proof that the audience's imagination had been switched on. The event's energetic format also ensured that listeners were engaged throughout and eager to participate once all the presentations had been completed.

Faysal Subhani and Kanwal Nayani, graduates of AKU's class of 2015, and CCIT core team members said: "We have been so encouraged by the response that we hope to host a Hackathon and a photo-focussed session, Photoignite in the year ahead."

Mayera Tufail (Year 3) and Huma Baqir (Year 4) are medical students at the Aga Khan University's Medical College in Karachi, Pakistan, and part of the core team of CCIT.
